title: CGM vs Fingerstick: Trust the Patient, Then Verify the Number
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: CGM values can lag behind blood glucose during rapid change and can occasionally be inaccurate. When symptoms do not match the sensor value or the device reports an error, confirm with the backup method specified in the treatment plan before making a high-risk treatment decision.
recognize: Rapid glucose change, sensor warm-up, compression, poor adhesion, expired sensor, dehydration, and device error can reduce confidence in a CGM reading.
priorities: Treat severe symptoms as real while obtaining confirmatory glucose when the plan/device instructions call for it.
assessMonitor: Compare symptoms, CGM trend arrows, recent insulin/food/activity, and confirmatory capillary glucose when indicated.
interventions: Follow the device-specific troubleshooting and diabetes action plan.
medicationSafety: Do not give repeated correction insulin solely from a questionable sensor value without verification when confirmation is required.
redFlags: Persistent severe high/low reading with symptoms
teaching: Keep an accessible backup glucose meter and supplies according to the diabetes plan.
delegationScope: Device setup/interpretation responsibilities depend on training and setting; urgent symptom escalation remains a licensed nursing responsibility.
examTrap: Ignoring neuroglycopenic symptoms because the CGM screen looks normal.
oneLinePearl: When symptoms and CGM disagree, verify—do not dismiss the patient.

title: Compression Lows: Pressure Can Falsely Lower CGM Readings
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Pressure on a CGM sensor, especially during sleep, can create falsely low readings in some systems. Assess symptoms and the trend pattern and use the plan's confirmatory method before repeated carbohydrate treatment when the reading seems implausible.
recognize: Abrupt overnight lows without symptoms that resolve after changing position can suggest compression artifact.
priorities: Check the patient first and confirm glucose when needed rather than repeatedly treating a likely artifact.
assessMonitor: Review sensor site, sleeping position, trend history, symptoms, and confirmatory glucose.
interventions: Relieve pressure and follow device troubleshooting instructions.
medicationSafety: Avoid reducing basal insulin or pump settings independently because of one suspected artifact.
teaching: Choose approved sensor sites and understand the device's troubleshooting guidance.
delegationScope: Routine observation may be shared; treatment-plan changes require authorized clinicians.
examTrap: Treating every isolated nighttime low sensor alarm as confirmed hypoglycemia without context.
oneLinePearl: A low alarm is a cue—symptoms and confirmation determine the next step.

title: CGM Sensor Failure: Switch to Backup Monitoring
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: If a CGM stops providing reliable data, diabetes treatment should continue using the prescribed backup glucose-monitoring method. Device failure is not a reason to stop insulin or ignore symptoms.
recognize: Signal loss, repeated errors, sensor detachment, implausible values, or prolonged missing data indicate unreliable monitoring.
priorities: Use backup glucose testing and maintain prescribed insulin while troubleshooting/replacing the sensor.
assessMonitor: Check symptoms, capillary glucose, device status, recent insulin, and illness/activity context.
interventions: Follow manufacturer replacement/troubleshooting instructions and notify the diabetes team when the plan requires.
medicationSafety: Do not stop basal insulin because CGM data are unavailable.
teaching: Always keep backup monitoring supplies available.
delegationScope: Device troubleshooting may be patient/caregiver driven; clinical deterioration requires licensed assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Waiting for a replacement sensor before checking glucose again.
oneLinePearl: When the sensor fails, monitoring changes—not the need for insulin.

title: Insulin Pump Interruption: Hyperglycemia Can Escalate Quickly
bottomLine: Many pump users receive rapid-acting insulin continuously, so prolonged interruption can produce marked hyperglycemia and ketosis faster than with long-acting basal regimens. Unexpected high glucose requires prompt pump/site assessment and the patient's backup plan.
recognize: Empty reservoir, dislodged cannula, occlusion, dead battery, tubing disconnect, damaged pump, or infusion-site failure can stop insulin delivery.
priorities: Check glucose, pump alarms, reservoir/tubing/site, and ketones when indicated by the action plan; use the prescribed backup insulin strategy.
assessMonitor: Trend glucose, symptoms, ketones when appropriate, last successful bolus, and device status.
interventions: Replace failed components/site per training and seek urgent diabetes-team/emergency care when hyperglycemia/ketosis persists.
medicationSafety: Do not repeatedly bolus through a suspected failed infusion site without confirming delivery.
teaching: Pump users need backup insulin, syringes/pens, glucose/ketone supplies, and written failure instructions.
delegationScope: Pump management requires training; hospital policies may restrict who changes settings or sites.
examTrap: Assuming the pump is delivering insulin because the screen is powered on.
oneLinePearl: A working screen does not prove insulin is reaching the patient.

title: Pump Infusion-Site Failure: High Glucose May Be a Delivery Problem
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Kinked cannulas, leakage, dislodgement, lipohypertrophy, bleeding, or site infection can impair insulin delivery even when the pump itself appears normal. Persistent unexplained hyperglycemia requires site assessment and action-plan troubleshooting.
recognize: Wet adhesive/insulin odor, loose set, pain, redness, swelling, blood in tubing, repeated highs, or lack of response to correction are cues.
priorities: Assess the infusion site/system and follow the backup/site-change plan; confirm glucose and ketones as directed.
assessMonitor: Check site integrity, glucose trend, ketones when indicated, pump alarms, and correction response.
interventions: Change the site/system per training when failure is suspected and use backup insulin if the plan directs.
medicationSafety: Do not stack repeated pump corrections through a site that may not be delivering insulin.
complications: Hypoglycemia if delayed insulin suddenly delivers
teaching: Rotate infusion sites and inspect them regularly.
delegationScope: Site changes/settings depend on patient competence and facility policy.
examTrap: Giving another pump bolus without checking the site after multiple failed corrections.
oneLinePearl: Persistent highs can mean the insulin never got in.

title: Sick-Day Device Safety: High Glucose Plus Ketones Needs Action
bottomLine: Illness can raise glucose and insulin needs while vomiting/dehydration increases DKA risk. Pump/CGM users should follow their sick-day plan, continue required basal insulin, check ketones when indicated, and escalate persistent hyperglycemia, vomiting, or ketosis.
recognize: Fever, infection, vomiting, pump interruption, rising glucose, thirst, polyuria, abdominal pain, or ketones are danger cues.
priorities: Assess hydration, glucose, ketones per plan, insulin delivery, and DKA symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend glucose, ketones, intake/output, vomiting, respiration, mental status, and device function.
interventions: Follow the prescribed sick-day correction/hydration/backup-insulin plan and seek urgent care for worsening ketosis or inability to hydrate.
medicationSafety: Do not stop basal insulin solely because the patient is not eating.
teaching: Keep written sick-day instructions and ketone-testing supplies available.
delegationScope: Sick-day plan implementation may be patient/caregiver managed; deterioration requires licensed assessment/emergency escalation.
examTrap: Stopping all insulin during vomiting because oral intake is poor.
oneLinePearl: Sick day means more monitoring—not no insulin.
sourceBasis: ADA sick-day and diabetes technology principles

title: Low-Glucose Alarm: Treat the Patient, Then Recheck
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A low-glucose alarm is a safety cue. If hypoglycemia is confirmed or symptoms are convincing, treat according to the patient's plan and reassess; severe neuroglycopenia requires emergency rescue rather than oral intake.
recognize: Sweating, tremor, hunger, confusion, behavior change, weakness, seizure, or unconsciousness can accompany hypoglycemia.
priorities: Determine whether the patient can safely swallow and use the prescribed fast-acting carbohydrate or rescue medication pathway.
assessMonitor: Recheck glucose after treatment per plan and identify likely cause such as excess insulin, delayed food, exercise, alcohol, or renal decline.
interventions: Use rescue glucagon/emergency response for severe hypoglycemia according to the plan and training.
medicationSafety: Do not give oral carbohydrate to an unconscious or unsafe-swallow patient.
teaching: Carry accessible treatment and ensure close contacts know rescue steps when appropriate.
delegationScope: Emergency assistance may be performed by trained caregivers/staff; medication authority follows policy.
examTrap: Giving juice to an unconscious patient because the glucose alarm is low.
oneLinePearl: Low glucose plus unsafe swallow means rescue—not oral sugar.

title: Automated Insulin Delivery: Automation Still Needs Oversight
bottomLine: Automated insulin-delivery systems can adjust insulin based on CGM data, but they still depend on functioning sensors, infusion delivery, meal input where required, and user response to alarms. Automation does not eliminate hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia, or device-failure risk.
recognize: Sensor failure, infusion interruption, missed meal announcements, algorithm limits, exercise, illness, and device alarms can all alter performance.
priorities: Respond to alarms and symptoms and use backup monitoring/insulin procedures when automation is unreliable.
assessMonitor: Review glucose trends, active insulin context, site/sensor status, and recent food/activity/illness.
interventions: Follow device-specific instructions rather than overriding settings without authorization.
medicationSafety: Do not assume the system will rescue every low or correct every high.
teaching: Know how to exit automation safely and use the backup plan when instructed.
delegationScope: Automated-delivery settings and troubleshooting require patient competence and facility/provider policy.
examTrap: Ignoring repeated alarms because the system is 'automatic.'
oneLinePearl: Automation reduces work; it does not remove vigilance.

title: Diabetes Devices: Do Not Share Patient-Dedicated Equipment
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Blood-glucose testing and insulin-delivery equipment can create infection and medication-safety risks when shared or reused improperly. Follow device labeling and facility infection-control rules for patient-dedicated equipment.
recognize: Fingerstick devices, lancets, insulin pens, reservoirs, and patient-contact components may not be safe for sharing even when visibly clean.
priorities: Use single-patient or single-use equipment as labeled and disinfect reusable meters according to approved instructions.
assessMonitor: Verify patient identity, device assignment, cleaning status, and supply integrity.
interventions: Remove mislabeled/shared equipment from use and report exposure risk according to policy.
medicationSafety: Insulin pens are patient specific and must not be shared between patients.
teaching: Do not share personal diabetes testing or injection devices.
delegationScope: Point-of-care testing may be delegated to trained staff under policy; infection-control rules still apply.
examTrap: Changing only the needle and sharing an insulin pen between patients.
oneLinePearl: New needle does not make a shared insulin pen safe.

title: Diabetes Technology Backup Plan: Assume Devices Can Fail
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Every person who depends on diabetes technology needs a practical backup plan for power loss, sensor/pump failure, travel, illness, and supply interruption. Backup monitoring and insulin instructions should be explicit before the failure occurs.
recognize: Dead battery, broken controller/phone, lost supplies, disaster evacuation, sensor shortage, or pump malfunction can interrupt diabetes management.
priorities: Ensure access to backup glucose testing, insulin delivery supplies/medication, emergency contacts, and written dosing instructions.
assessMonitor: Review backup-supply availability, expiration, storage, charging/power needs, and patient/caregiver competence.
interventions: Reinforce the diabetes team's device-failure and emergency plan.
medicationSafety: Backup insulin regimens must be prescribed and understood; do not invent conversion doses during device failure.
redFlags: No backup insulin for pump-dependent patient
teaching: Keep backup supplies where they remain usable during travel or emergencies and review the plan periodically.
delegationScope: Emergency-plan teaching may be reinforced by the PN/LVN within the established plan; dose changes require authorized prescriber/team input.
examTrap: Assuming the pharmacy or clinic will always be immediately reachable when the device fails.
oneLinePearl: Technology is safest when failure has already been planned for.
